name: Georgism
summary: Georgism, from the American economist Henry George, holds that people own what they produce but that land and natural resources belong to everyone, so the rent they yield should go to the community. Its main policy is a tax on the unimproved value of land that would replace taxes on labor, capital and trade, leaving land in private hands while socializing its rent. It pairs this with free trade and opposition to monopoly privilege, and some adherents would return surplus rent as a citizen's dividend.
scope: Classical Georgism as set out in Henry George's own books, speeches and journalism (Progress and Poverty 1879, The Land Question 1881, Social Problems 1883, Protection or Free Trade 1886, the 1887 Standard essay on socialism, A Perplexed Philosopher 1892), read with the scholarship on the single-tax movement. Modern Georgist organisations are used only where they state a position as their own. It excludes the anarchist and proprietary-community offshoots (Nock, Heath, MacCallum) and borrows nothing from the wider left, liberal or libertarian camps that have drawn on George.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: He says the American republic could dispense with both army and navy, keeping only frontier police, though he calls this a matter for that republic.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: He treats division of labor as the source of production's advances and describes its advantages as soon apparent.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He treats the abolition of hereditary privileges and legal class distinctions in the United States as an achievement.

abolish-ip.rationale: The corrected note in Progress and Poverty VIII.3 distinguishes patents, which restrict others’ independent use of ideas, from copyright protection of an author’s actual labour. He does not abolish both together.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: He denies that the wage system is inherently unjust: with land open to labor, the evils of wages would disappear without abolishing them.

arms-reduction.rationale: He argues that standing armies and navies are inimical to democracy and costly in peace.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: He calls public debt an evil that lets tyrants and wars be financed, and says costs should be met by taxation as they arise.

ban-cartels.rationale: He says the labor party proposes to break up all monopolies, though by removing privilege and public management rather than a general ban.

ban-interest.rationale: In Progress and Poverty he sets out the reason and justification of interest as a legitimate earning of capital and opposes the view that it is robbery.

basic-income.rationale: He lists dividing surplus rent among the community share and share alike as one use of the common fund, and a modern Georgist body says land rent is the best funding for a basic income.

central-planning.rationale: He calls state direction of all production and exchange impracticable and likely to end in anarchy or despotism.

character-from-environment.rationale: He argues that differences in civilization come from social organisation rather than innate traits, and that heredity counts for little beside what moulds a person after birth.

class-collaboration.rationale: He says the evils of labor do not arise from conflict between labor and capital, whose relation he calls one of conjunction rather than opposition.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: He describes British rule in India as that of an absentee alien landlord draining the people.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: His law of progress holds that progress comes from association in equality, and that conflict wastes the mental power progress needs, though he values free competition in production (Progress and Poverty, book X).

consent-of-governed.rationale: He opens The Land Question with the Declaration of Independence's claim that just powers come from the consent of the governed.

corporate-influence.rationale: He describes railroad and other combinations buying legislatures and lobbying for profitable favours.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: He rejects state regulation of wages and prices as beyond the state's power, which excludes state-recognised bodies setting both.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: He would abolish all customs, excise, license and other taxes on production and exchange and rely on land rent.

decide-locally.rationale: He urges local self-government for matters that concern only each township, ward, city or state, while noting that uniformity grows with scale.

delink-world-market.rationale: His case for free trade applies to poor and rich countries alike; he never treats integration into world trade as a trap.

democracy-best.rationale: He holds that the ultimate power lies with the masses and values democratic government, while warning that it decays into despotism where wealth is concentrated.

distribution-by-process.rationale: His argument is that what a man produces is rightfully his and that unequal wealth is unjust because it arises from monopoly of land and privilege.

dynastic-succession.rationale: He holds hereditary succession to power to be an inheritance of feudal privilege that a democratic republic has swept away.

economic-freedom.rationale: He says democratic government in more than name needs wealth distributed with something like equality, so that citizens are not dependent on a master.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: He argues that nations gain by exchange and that restriction of trade only makes nations rivals, so a bloc shut off from outside trade is the opposite of his case.

elective-rulers.rationale: He praises a republic in which every official depends on popular vote and attacks divine right.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He builds his case on the equal and unalienable rights of all men, and says no law or custom can justify denying them.

flat-income-tax.rationale: The proposed remedy removes income taxation rather than recommending a flat income-tax rate.

free-trade.rationale: George holds that free trade, carried to its logical end, benefits all nations and workers, but that tariff removal alone cannot lastingly raise wages while land monopoly captures the gains (Protection or Free Trade, chapters XXV-XXVI).

harm-principle.rationale: He says government should be repressive no further than is needed to protect each person's equal rights from aggression, and it is not its business to make men virtuous.

hereditarian-race.rationale: He says differences between peoples cannot be ascribed to innate differences in individuals and treats supposed racial inferiority as a product of treatment.

homestead-ownership.rationale: George calls deriving an exclusive and perpetual title to land from first occupation the most absurd defence of land ownership, since each generation has the same right.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: He holds that wages and interest are earnings while rent for mere ownership of land is not, though he defends returns to capital.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: He sees modern progress producing want beside wealth, but as correctable injustice that could bring a golden age.

land-redistribution.rationale: He rejects dividing land among the people as impossible to maintain and proposes taking rent for the community instead, leaving possession as it is.

land-use-tenure.rationale: George says land must be made common property, but leaves possession, sale and inheritance to individuals who pay its rent to the community; title does not depend on personal use.

land-value-tax.rationale: The single tax is George's central remedy: abolish taxes on labor, capital and exchange and take land rent for the public in a tax on land value.

limit-population.rationale: He says the earth could support far more people, that Nature provides for all, and he rejects the prudential checks urged by Malthus and Besant.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: He says free competition through supply and demand would fix returns and the kinds and amounts of goods better than any board of statisticians could.

military-superiority.rationale: He calls the US navy a burlesque and says the nation is too strong to be attacked and ought to be too great to attack others.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: He speaks of the democratic tendency's remaining triumphs as sweeping away the vestiges of monarchy, aristocracy and prelacy.

nation-first.rationale: He says protection makes nations rivals instead of co-operators and denies that the interests of nations are opposed.

national-church-status.rationale: He applauds the sweeping away of prelacy alongside monarchy and aristocracy as political privilege.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He says only in the infancy of society can government be confined to defence and protection, and cooperative functions must be added.

no-business-privileges.rationale: He attacks tariffs, patents, franchises, subsidies and land grants as privileges that make the favoured rich.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: He says rings, bosses and the lobbying power of wealth have corrupted American government and taken it out of the people's hands.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: He rejects the Malthusian doctrine and says poverty is due to institutions, not population pressure.

positive-liberty.rationale: He holds that a man dependent on an employer for living is not free, and that freedom to earn should go with freedom to vote.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: He says attempts to lower the price of goods by regulation have always ended by raising it.

profit-exploitation.rationale: He rejects the Marxian theory that profits are surplus value withheld from workers, treating interest as a return that arises from capital's increase.

property-fundamental.rationale: He holds property in the products of labor to be sacred but denies that land can be property, so his doctrine splits by kind of property.

public-money-creation.rationale: He says a note issued directly by the government is as good as one based on a bond and calls the hybrid bank currency a creature of private profit.

public-ownership.rationale: He holds that railroads, telegraphs, telephones and the supply of gas, water, heat and electricity are monopolies that belong to the state.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: He says the state cannot cure poverty by regulating wages, any more than it can regulate interest, because wages are fixed by access to land.

rent-control.rationale: He argues that courts fixing a fair rent only let the tenant charge a successor more, and a modern Georgist body says law can only decide who receives the rent.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: The core claim is that every person has an equal right to the earth, so individuals who hold land owe its rental value to the community.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: He says the only course consistent with American institutions is to leave abuses of speech to their natural remedy short of direct incitement to specific illegal acts.

return-to-foraging.rationale: He calls civilization man's natural destiny and says only a mood of envying cud-chewing cattle could regret the savage state.

sacred-ruler.rationale: He calls the divine right of kings a blasphemy and a monstrous doctrine.

self-ownership.rationale: He grounds property in a man's right to himself and his powers, so what a man produces is his own against all the world.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: He denies that one generation can bind another by debt and calls the enforced Egyptian debt a flagrant spoliation.

state-directs-investment.rationale: He holds that governmental direction in place of individual action is defective, and that free competition allocates better than any bureau.

state-harmful.rationale: He holds government to be necessary for justice and for cooperative functions, and to be reformed not removed.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Protection or Free Trade? is a sustained argument that tariffs impoverish a country and mainly serve monopolists.

tax-inheritance.rationale: He lists taxes on legacies and successions with income and customs taxes as morally no better than highway robbery.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: George called income and succession taxes aimed at the rich a violation of property, but Georgists later backed the progressive income tax as a step toward the single tax.

taxation-theft.rationale: He calls taxes on labor, income and legacies robbery but holds that taxing the rental value of land is just.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: His central claim is that material progress alone does not abolish poverty and enriches landowners until land is common property.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He condemns wars of rapine among unoffending peoples and wants no wanton attack on other nations.

trade-surplus.rationale: He calls the idea that an excess of exports over imports shows enrichment an absurdity, and cites Rome's provinces, whose export surplus marked their impoverishment.

unions-good.rationale: George says unions can raise wages only by force at the expense of other workers and cannot lift wages generally, yet credits them with shorter hours and higher pay in some trades.

universal-morality.rationale: He holds that moral law stands above human law and custom, so that the equal right to life and land is valid whatever laws or customs say.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: He quotes Aquinas that human law deviating from right reason is not law but violence, and applies it to property granted by the state.

war-builds-character.rationale: He says war and military glory pervert social instincts into miscalled patriotism and dull public conscience.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: He says monstrous fortunes and corporate wealth mean loss of governmental control by the people and democratic forms hide tyranny.

workers-own-party.rationale: He helped found a labor party in 1887 and argued that its platform must stand apart from state socialism.

missingStatements.text: A community that takes the rental value of land for public use owes no compensation to the landowners.
missingStatements.rationale: George says any proposal to compensate landlords is a proposal to do a fresh wrong and that the resumption of all land would treat owners equally.

missingStatements.text: One generation cannot bind later generations by public debts or by land titles.
missingStatements.rationale: He argues that public debts and land titles alike rest on the false assumption that ascendants may bind descendants.

missingStatements.text: Government should operate businesses that are by nature monopolies, such as railroads, telegraphs and water and gas supply, while leaving other industry to free competition.
missingStatements.rationale: He holds that such businesses are properly functions of the state and that competition elsewhere allocates better than any bureau.

notes:
Georgists split between a 'single tax limited' strand that would raise only what government needs and an 'unlimited' strand that would take all land rent. Domitrovic reports that Georgists later backed the progressive income tax and public ownership beyond the single tax, which George's own 1892 text condemns for income taxes; tax-the-wealthy is therefore recorded as a split. Themes searched in George's full texts: economy, government, society, world, liberty, culture, ecology, technology, means, globalism. George's own texts record no position on immigration levels (his 1880 remarks and Protection or Free Trade treat Chinese labor competition only as a source of discontent and as a wage effect under present conditions), women's suffrage, the death penalty, drugs, abortion or sexuality, so those are null. A 2026-10-14 pass answered many such questions by inference; this pass keeps only stated positions and drops the old free-trade-adjacent and land-claims answers that rested on general values, including indigenous land authority and the earlier immigration, gradualism and social-issue answers.

Merged with an independent claude-opus-5-5+GPT-6.1-Sol audit: 4 answers taken from it, 15 agreed, 4 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-opus-5-5+GPT-6.1-Sol notes: Independent reconstruction from source leads, not previous answers. Full primary books downloaded and searched across taxes/land/capital, government/democracy, war and international trade, social policy, race/religion, science/technology, nature and means. The full trade text was retrieved locally with certificate verification disabled after browser access failed. Crucially, trade freedom does not establish a stance on international organizations, binding labour/environment clauses or open borders. Equal natural-resource rights do not determine historical territorial claims or Indigenous sovereignty. The free-trade statement receives qualified disagreement because its literal everyone-benefits claim is expressly rejected for tariff removal without land reform; this is not an endorsement of protection. No inclusion padding from a wider libertarian or progressive camp.
